narrative:
The model predicted a 77% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were by far the strongest influence, and both pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the second decile after your first year and the bottom decile after your third year, compared with an average around the sixth and fifth-to-sixth deciles among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings signaled to the model a high risk that you would struggle with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score of 36 was the second most important factor. While this score is only slightly below the 37.2 average of accepted students, it still nudged the prediction modestly toward passing.

Your family income bracket (middle) was the third most important feature. It pushed the outcome slightly toward failure, though its effect was much smaller than your academic rankings.

Given these results, the clearest path forward is to strengthen your academic record. Retaking courses to improve your GPA, preparing intensively for a higher LSAT score, or gaining structured study support could meaningfully raise your chances on a future application. Focus first on the areas that most directly affect bar exam readiness. (218 words)
